Stroke nutritional management


Nutritional Management and Treatment
Use of modiﬁed food textures and ﬂuid consistencies aims to reduce the level of challenge posed in terms of manipulation of the
food bolus (i.e., by reducing the numbers of different textures presented and increasing the viscosity) and to alter the rate at which it
passes through the pharynx, to maximize patient control of swallowing and reduce the risk of aspiration. National professional
groups world-wide have developed classiﬁcation systems for modiﬁcation in the texture and consistency of foods and ﬂuids. These
usually cite approximately three grades, e.g., soft, minced, and pureed foods; mildly, moderately, and extremely thickened ﬂuids
(Tables 3–7).
It is commonly the responsibility of the speech pathologist to recommend the most appropriate food textures and maneuvers to
promote safe eating for a dysphagic stroke patient (Tables 4 and 8). Dietitians ensure that texture-modiﬁed meals are adequate to
meet nutrient requirements, offer choice, and are palatable. Skilled nursing assistance and interventions at mealtimes can also aid
